Censorship is the act of blocking, suppressing, or controlling information, speech, art, or any form of communication — usually by someone in a position of power — so that other people cannot freely access, share, or express it.

Think of it this way: imagine you write a letter, but before it reaches the person you sent it to, someone intercepts it, reads it, and tears out the parts they don't want the reader to see. That act of blocking information is censorship.
What exactly gets censored?

Almost anything can be censored. Common targets include:

  • Books, newspapers, and articles — written content that challenges authority, spreads uncomfortable truths, or questions the powerful
  • Art and music — paintings, songs, or films that are seen as offensive, immoral, or politically dangerous
  • Speech and opinions — what people say in public, in protests, on radio, or on television
  • The internet and social media — websites blocked, posts removed, or entire platforms banned
  • News — stories about government failures, wars, or scandals that those in power don't want people to know about
  • Scientific or academic ideas — theories or findings that conflict with religious doctrine or state ideology

The target is always the same: information or expression that someone with power wants to keep away from others.
Who does the censoring?

The agent of censorship — called a censor — can be:

  • A government or state: This is the most classic and powerful form. A government may censor media, restrict the internet, or ban books to keep citizens from learning things that could lead to protest or revolution. Countries like North Korea and China are well-known for extensive state censorship.
  • A religious institution: Throughout history, churches and religious authorities have banned books and ideas they considered heretical or dangerous to faith.
  • A corporation or platform: A company may remove content from its platform — not because a law forces it, but because it violates their own rules or damages their reputation.
  • Schools or parents: Restricting what children can read or learn about is also a form of censorship, though people debate whether it's protective or harmful.
  • The military: Governments often censor information during wartime so that military strategies aren't revealed to the enemy.
Why does censorship happen?

People who carry out censorship always have a reason — or at least a justification. Common ones include:

  • National security: "This information could help our enemies or endanger our troops."
  • Public order: "This will incite riots, hatred, or violence."
  • Morality: "This is obscene, indecent, or corrupting to society — especially to children."
  • Political control: "This threatens the authority of the government or the ruling group." (This is where censorship becomes most controversial.)
  • Protection of reputation: "This is false and damaging to us."
  • Religious reasons: "This offends our faith or contradicts sacred beliefs."

It's worth noting that not everyone who censors believes they are doing something wrong. Many censors genuinely believe they are protecting people. The disagreement is whether that protection is legitimate or whether it is an abuse of power.
Two key types of censorship

1. Pre-censorship (also called prior restraint):
This happens before information reaches the public. A government reviews a book before it's published and orders changes or a ban. A film is stopped before it's released. A journalist is prevented from broadcasting a story. This is generally considered the most severe form, because the public never even gets a chance to encounter the information.

2. Post-censorship:
This happens after information has been made public. A book is burned or banned after it's already been circulating. A post is removed from social media. A song is pulled from radio stations. This is more common today, especially online, and is somewhat less absolute — some people may have already seen or heard the content.
Self-censorship: censorship from within

There is a quieter, subtler form called self-censorship. This is when a person or organization voluntarily holds back information or expression — not because someone is physically forcing them, but because they fear punishment, ridicule, job loss, or other consequences.

A journalist who avoids writing about a powerful politician because they're afraid of being fired is self-censoring. A teacher who doesn't discuss a controversial topic because they fear parental complaints is self-censoring. This is considered especially damaging because it is invisible — no one has to order you to be silent; fear does the job instead.
Censorship vs. related things that people confuse it with

Censorship vs. editing:
When an editor removes sentences from your article to improve it, that is not censorship. Censorship is specifically about suppressing ideas because of their content — because they are politically threatening, morally inconvenient, or dangerous to someone's power. Editing is about quality, clarity, and accuracy.

Censorship vs. consequences:
If you say something publicly and people criticize you, boycott you, or refuse to give you a platform, that is generally not censorship — that is social accountability. Censorship involves a power imbalance where an authority prevents you from speaking in the first place or removes your speech after the fact. The line here is debated, but the key is: are you being silenced by someone with coercive power over you?

Censorship vs. content moderation:
This is a genuinely contested area. When a social media company removes hateful posts, some call it censorship, others call it responsible moderation. The difference often comes down to: who is doing it, what their power is, and whether the removal is proportionate and transparent.
Why censorship is controversial

Censorship sits right at the heart of one of humanity's oldest arguments: freedom of expression vs. protection from harm.

On one side: free expression is fundamental. People have a right to think, speak, write, and share ideas without interference. Censorship — even well-intentioned censorship — risks being abused to silence dissent, protect corrupt power, and prevent people from accessing truth. History is full of examples where censored books turned out to be important, revolutionary, or simply true.

On the other side: some speech causes real, measurable harm — hate speech that leads to violence, misinformation during a pandemic that kills people, child exploitation material. A completely uncensored world is not necessarily a free world; it can be a world where the loudest and most harmful voices drown out everything else.

Most modern democracies try to strike a balance: strong free speech protections with narrow, well-defined limits — though where exactly to draw that line is endlessly debated.
A few memorable examples

• In Nazi Germany, the regime burned books by Jewish authors, political opponents, and anyone whose ideas conflicted with their ideology.
  • Index Librorum Prohibitorum was the Catholic Church's official list of banned books, which ran for centuries and included works by Galileo and many other thinkers.
  • The Great Firewall of China is a massive internet censorship system that blocks access to Google, Facebook, Twitter, Wikipedia, and thousands of websites for over a billion people.
  • In the Soviet Union, all media was state-controlled; unauthorized publications were banned, and writers who disobeyed were imprisoned or exiled.
  • In the United States, books like The Catcher in the Rye, To Kill a Mockingbird, and Harry Potter have been banned or challenged in various school districts over the decades — a milder form, but structurally the same act.
Summary

Censorship is the suppression or control of information, expression, or ideas by a person or institution with power. It happens for many reasons — security, morality, politics, religion — and takes many forms, from outright bans and book burnings to quiet internet blocks and fearful self-silencing. It is one of the most powerful tools of control ever used by governments and institutions, and one of the most enduring battles in human history has been the fight against it. Understanding censorship means understanding both why it happens and what is lost when information is kept from people who might need it.
